newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog no comment on brokerage raid report.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog no comment on brokerage raid report.

text.p: Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), said on Monday that it would not comment on Japanese media reports over the weekend that it had raided three major brokerages.
"We cannot and will not answer such a question," an SESC official said.

The Japanese newspaper Sankei Shimbun reported on Saturday that the SESC went to the three securities houses -- Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd -- to investigate possible wrongdoing.

The Kyodo news service reported on Saturday that the SESC "has raided the offices of three major Japanese brokerages in search of evidence" that they gave favours to a racketeer, the same person involved in a scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd .
Spokesmen at Yamaichi and Nikko declined to comment on the reports.

The Daiwa spokesman repeated a statement made by the company last month that the SESC has been conducting inspections since March 3 but that the firm believed the checks were routine and not related to any suspicious deals.

The Nomura scandal surfaced on March 6 when the company, Japan's biggest brokerage, said internal probes had found that directors had made improper deals and funnelled profits raised through stock trading to a corporate client run by a relative of the racketeer.

A government source said it would be normal for the SESC to try to get information from the three brokerages after Japanese media reports saying that the same racketeer involved in the Nomura scandal had accounts at the firms.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said last month he believed the SESC would likely investigate the three companies, who together with Nomura constitute the "Big Four" Japanese financial houses.
"It's hard to believe the authorities will sit by after such reports. It's common sense for them to conduct an appropriate investigation," he said.
He added: "I think the SESC and the Finance Ministry will move to see whether there are links as reported." But Mitsuzuka did not clarify whether any formal investigation was planned.
